exam: What is the first step in managing a patient with suspected brain herniation? — Secure airway, elevate head, give hyperosmolar therapy.

How would you differentiate a transtentorial herniation from a subfalcine herniation on imaging? — Look for uncal herniation of the temporal lobe and compression of the midbrain versus compression of the falx and frontal lobes.
Why is a lumbar puncture avoided in a patient with a fixed, dilated pupil? — Risk of precipitating herniation by lowering CSF pressure.
Which infection is most likely to cause a cerebral abscess in a malaria‑endemic area? — Tuberculosis, often presenting as a tuberculoma.
What is the significance of a midline shift >10 mm on CT? — Indicates severe herniation requiring urgent decompression.
Which drug should be avoided in a patient with raised ICP and renal failure? — Mannitol, due to risk of volume overload and renal toxicity.
ai.title: Brain Herniation Pathology
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Brain herniation is a life‑threatening displacement of brain tissue through a skull defect or foramen, usually due to raised intracranial pressure. Rapid recognition and treatment are essential.

b: Raised ICP, focal neurological signs, altered consciousness
sections.p: Brain herniation occurs when increased intracranial pressure forces brain tissue across a natural or surgical barrier. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by imaging when available.

t.b: Detects herniation type and mass effect; a midline shift >5 mm suggests significant herniation.
Shows detailed brain anatomy and herniation; used when CT is inconclusive.
Papilledema indicates chronic raised ICP; optic disc swelling may precede herniation.

b: Grade I – mild symptoms, no imaging evidence of herniation
Grade II – focal deficits, imaging shows small herniation
Grade III – severe deficits, large herniation, midline shift >10 mm
Grade IV – coma, brainstem herniation, imminent death
sections.p: The World Health Organization (WHO) grading for brain herniation is based on clinical status and imaging findings.
In low‑resource settings, the leading causes are infections, trauma, and space‑occupying lesions.
Symptoms evolve with the type of herniation; early signs are non‑specific, progressing to focal deficits and brainstem signs.
